lessons.title: How Networks Move Data: Packets, Frames & the OSI Model

slots.practicalActivity: On your own machine, open a browser's DevTools Network tab (or run curl -v against a real site) while loading one real webpage, and write out, piece by piece, how that single request gets encapsulated on its way out: the HTTP request (Application), wrapped in a TCP segment with port numbers (Transport), wrapped in an IP packet with your machine's and the server's addresses (Network), wrapped in an Ethernet frame with MAC addresses (Data Link), down to bits on the wire (Physical). Then write the bottom-up troubleshooting order the lesson gives (Physical → Data Link → Network → Transport → Application) and explain, in your own words, why checking the cable before the app actually saves time.
slots.deliverable: A written encapsulation trace (Application → Transport → Network → Data Link → Physical) for one real webpage request captured via curl -v or DevTools, plus the bottom-up troubleshooting order explained in your own words.

lessons.title: The TCP/IP Model & How It Maps to OSI

slots.practicalActivity: Run curl -v against a real HTTPS site and identify, in the connection log, exactly where TCP's three-way handshake (SYN/SYN-ACK/ACK) completes before any HTTP data moves. Then build a 4-row table mapping the TCP/IP model's four layers to the matching OSI layers from last lesson, and for 3 real applications you choose yourself (e.g. a video call, a file download, a DNS lookup), decide whether each one is almost certainly using TCP or UDP and justify each choice in one sentence.
slots.deliverable: curl -v output with the TCP handshake identified, a completed TCP/IP-to-OSI mapping table, and a 3-row TCP-vs-UDP classification with a one-sentence justification for each of 3 real applications.

lessons.title: IP Addressing & Subnetting Fundamentals

slots.practicalActivity: By hand, work out the network address, first/last usable host, and broadcast address for 192.168.1.0/27, matching the lesson's worked example, then repeat the full calculation for 10.0.5.0/28 using the 2^(host bits)-2 formula. Finally, run ipconfig /all (Windows) or ip addr (Linux/Mac) on your own machine, find your real IP address and subnet mask, and convert that mask to its CIDR notation.
slots.deliverable: Two fully worked subnet calculations (192.168.1.0/27 and 10.0.5.0/28) showing network, host range, and broadcast addresses, plus your own machine's real IP address and subnet mask converted to CIDR notation.

lessons.title: IPv4 vs. IPv6

slots.practicalActivity: Run ipconfig /all or ip addr on your own machine and find both your real IPv4 address and your real IPv6 address if one is assigned. Take the address 2001:0db8:85a3:0000:0000:8a2e:0370:7334 and apply both IPv6 shorthand rules yourself — drop leading zeros, then collapse the longest run of all-zero groups with :: — showing each step. Then write 2-3 sentences explaining what dual-stack means and whether your own machine is already running it.
slots.deliverable: Your own machine's real IPv4 and IPv6 addresses, a step-by-step shorthand reduction of the given IPv6 address, and a written explanation of dual-stack using your own machine as the example.

lessons.title: Common Network Ports & Protocols You'll See Daily

slots.practicalActivity: Without looking at the lesson's table, write the standard port number for all 11 protocols it lists from memory, then check your answers against the lesson. On your own machine, run netstat -an (Windows/Mac) or ss -tuln (Linux) and find at least 3 real ports your machine is currently listening on or connected through, naming the well-known protocol for each one you recognize. Finally, run curl -v against a real HTTPS site and point out your machine's ephemeral source port in the output.
slots.deliverable: An 11-row self-test of port numbers scored against the lesson, netstat/ss output identifying at least 3 real local ports, and curl -v output showing your machine's ephemeral source port for one real HTTPS connection.

lessons.title: Switches, Routers & How Traffic Actually Flows

slots.practicalActivity: On your own machine, run arp -a to see the real MAC-to-IP mappings your machine has learned on its local subnet — the same job a switch's MAC address table does — then run ip route (Linux/WSL) or route print / netstat -r (Windows/Mac) to see your own routing table and identify your default gateway. Using the lesson's Host A → Host B walkthrough as a model, write your own 4-step narration of what happens when your machine sends a request to a real external site, naming exactly where the MAC address changes and where the IP address stays the same.
slots.deliverable: Your machine's real ARP table and routing table output with the default gateway identified, plus a written 4-step walkthrough of a packet leaving your subnet, correctly noting where the MAC address changes and where the IP address doesn't.

lessons.title: DNS: How Names Become Addresses

slots.practicalActivity: Run dig (or nslookup on Windows) against 3 real domains you choose, capturing the A record, its TTL, and at least one MX or TXT record for one of them, and note whether each answer is marked non-authoritative. Then write a short scenario: a domain's TTL is 86400 seconds and its owner needs to migrate it to a new server starting tomorrow — explain what they should do to the TTL today, and why, so the cutover doesn't leave some users on the old IP for a full day.
slots.deliverable: dig/nslookup output for 3 real domains showing an A record, TTL, and at least one MX/TXT record, plus a written explanation of why and how to lower a TTL in advance of a real migration.

lessons.title: DHCP & Dynamic IP Assignment

slots.practicalActivity: Run ipconfig /all (Windows) or check your network settings (Mac/Linux) to find your own real DHCP lease details — your assigned IP, the DHCP server's address, and the lease obtained/expiration times. Then write out the full 4-step DORA exchange (Discover, Offer, Request, Acknowledge) narrated specifically for your own device joining your network this morning, and explain in one sentence why a server or printer on the same network would more likely be given a static IP instead.
slots.deliverable: Your own machine's real DHCP lease details (IP, DHCP server, lease times), a written DORA walkthrough narrated for your own device, and a one-sentence explanation of when a static IP is the better choice.

lessons.title: NAT, Firewalls & Basic Network Security Concepts

slots.practicalActivity: Find your own machine's private IP (ipconfig/ifconfig) and public IP (search "what is my IP"), and explain in your own words how NAT/PAT is the specific mechanism translating between the two every time you reach the internet. Then write a 3-rule ACL, in the lesson's exact permit/deny/port format, that allows HTTPS from your own private subnet, blocks Telnet from anywhere, and denies everything else by default — and explain why rule order matters given that the first match wins.
slots.deliverable: Your own real private/public IP pair with a written NAT/PAT explanation, plus a 3-rule ACL written in the lesson's permit/deny format with an explanation of why first-match-wins ordering matters.

lessons.title: Why Linux Runs the Cloud
lessons.chapterTitle: Linux Fundamentals I — The Shell & Filesystem

slots.practicalActivity: Set up a real Linux environment you'll use for the rest of this course — WSL2 with Ubuntu (Windows) or a VirtualBox Ubuntu Server VM (any OS) — and once it's running, run uname -a and cat /etc/os-release to confirm the exact kernel version and distro. Then open a free-tier AWS, Azure, or GCP console and browse its VM image catalog, naming 3 real Linux distro options you see offered and noting which one appears as the default.
slots.deliverable: A working Linux lab environment (WSL2 or a VirtualBox VM) with real uname -a and /etc/os-release output, plus 3 real Linux distro options found in a cloud provider's VM catalog with the default one noted.

lessons.title: The Linux Filesystem Hierarchy
lessons.chapterTitle: Linux Fundamentals I — The Shell & Filesystem

slots.practicalActivity: On your lab machine, run ls -la / to see the real top-level directory tree, then explore 5 of the directories from the lesson's table yourself (ls /etc, ls /var/log, ls /home, ls /usr, ls /tmp) and write one real sentence for each describing what you actually found there. Finally, imagine a coworker says a service crashed overnight with no other details — write which directory you'd check first and why, per the lesson.
slots.deliverable: Real ls -la / output from your lab machine, 5 written sentences describing what you actually found in /etc, /var/log, /home, /usr, and /tmp, plus a one-sentence answer naming /var/log as the first troubleshooting stop.

lessons.title: Essential Shell Commands for Navigation & Files
lessons.chapterTitle: Linux Fundamentals I — The Shell & Filesystem

slots.practicalActivity: On your lab machine, run pwd and ls -la to see where you are, then mkdir a backups directory, touch a file inside it, cp another file into it, mv/rename something, and finally rm -r the whole directory to clean up. Create a sample log file with at least 10 lines, use grep -i -r to search for a keyword inside it, and use find /var/log -name "*.log" -mtime -1 to find recently modified files. Finally use less to page through a longer file, searching inside it with /.
slots.deliverable: Terminal output showing pwd/ls -la, a full mkdir/touch/cp/mv/rm -r cycle on a real backups directory, a grep -i -r search of a sample log file, a find command filtered by name and modification time, and a less session with a search performed inside it.

lessons.title: Linux Users, Groups & Permissions
lessons.chapterTitle: Linux Fundamentals I — The Shell & Filesystem

slots.practicalActivity: On your lab machine, create a new group with sudo groupadd, create a new user with sudo useradd -m -s /bin/bash, set its password with passwd, and add it to the new group with sudo usermod -aG, confirming membership with groups. Then run ls -l against 3 of your own files, read out each full rwx permission string, and use chmod in both octal (755) and symbolic (u+x) mode on different files, confirming each change with ls -l. Finally, use sudo chown to change one file's owner and group.
slots.deliverable: A newly created user and group on your lab machine confirmed with groups, plus ls -l output for 3 files before and after chmod changes made in both octal and symbolic notation, and one file with its owner/group changed via chown.

lessons.title: Package Management (apt, yum & dnf)
lessons.chapterTitle: Linux Fundamentals I — The Shell & Filesystem

slots.practicalActivity: On your lab machine, run apt update, then apt search for a real package you don't have installed (e.g. htop), install it with apt install, confirm it's installed with apt list --installed | grep, and remove it with apt remove. If your lab runs an RHEL-family distro instead, run the equivalent dnf check-update/search/install/remove sequence. Write one sentence comparing the exact command differences between the two families for the same 5 tasks in the lesson's comparison table.
slots.deliverable: A real package searched for, installed, confirmed, and removed using apt or dnf on your lab machine, with the exact commands and output captured, plus a one-sentence comparison of the apt vs. dnf command shapes.

lessons.title: Processes, Services & systemd

slots.practicalActivity: On your lab machine, run ps aux | grep for a real running process (e.g. sshd) and note its PID, then run top (or install htop) to watch live CPU/memory usage. Start a long-running dummy process (sleep 300 &), find its PID, send it a plain kill (SIGTERM) and confirm it stopped, then start another and practice kill -9 (SIGKILL) on it. Finally, run systemctl status on a real service, stop/start/restart it, and check systemctl enable/disable to see whether it's set to survive a reboot.
slots.deliverable: Real ps aux output identifying a process's PID, a kill (SIGTERM) and a kill -9 (SIGKILL) each demonstrated on a dummy background process, plus systemctl status/stop/start/restart/enable output for one real service on your lab machine.

lessons.title: SSH: Remote Access & Key-Based Authentication

slots.practicalActivity: Generate a real SSH key pair on your own machine with ssh-keygen -t ed25519, then install the public key onto your lab VM — via ssh-copy-id if connecting from a separate host, or by manually appending it to ~/.ssh/authorized_keys with the correct chmod 700/600 permissions if the VM is local. Confirm you can log in with ssh user@host and no password prompt, then write 2-3 sentences explaining, in your own words, why possessing only the public key would never be enough for someone else to log in as you.
slots.deliverable: A real SSH key pair generated and installed on your lab VM, proven by a no-password login, plus a written explanation of why a stolen public key alone can't be used to log in.

lessons.title: Linux Logs & Where to Look When Something Breaks

slots.practicalActivity: On your lab machine, pick a real service (e.g. sshd or the unit from last lesson) and run the lesson's exact 3-step workflow against it: systemctl status <service>, then journalctl -u <service> -n 50, then tail -f /var/log/syslog (or /var/log/messages) while you restart the service in a second terminal to watch new lines appear live. Finally, run grep -i error against /var/log/syslog and tail -n 100 /var/log/auth.log | grep "Failed password" to practice filtering.
slots.deliverable: Real output from the 3-step troubleshooting workflow (systemctl status, journalctl -u, and a tail -f session captured during a live restart) run against one real service, plus a grep -i error search and a filtered auth.log check for failed logins.

lessons.title: Shell Scripting Basics for Automation

slots.practicalActivity: Write a real check-services.sh script on your lab machine with a #!/bin/bash shebang, a SERVICE variable, an if/else block using systemctl is-active --quiet to report whether that service is running, and a for loop that tails the last 5 lines of 2 real log files. Run it first with bash check-services.sh, then chmod +x it and run it again with ./check-services.sh, confirming both methods produce the same output.
slots.deliverable: A real, executable check-services.sh script with a shebang, a variable, an if/else service check, and a for loop over 2 log files, run successfully both via bash and via ./ after chmod +x.

lessons.title: What Virtualization Actually Is: Type 1 vs. Type 2 Hypervisors

slots.practicalActivity: Install Oracle VirtualBox (a Type 2 hypervisor) if you haven't already, and create one VM inside it, noting that your own laptop's host OS keeps running underneath it the whole time. Then research one real Type 1 hypervisor an employer might actually run (VMware ESXi, Microsoft Hyper-V Server, or KVM) and write 2-3 sentences explaining why that hypervisor runs with no host OS underneath it, and why that absence is exactly what gives it near-native performance.
slots.deliverable: A real VM created in VirtualBox (Type 2) with a note confirming the host OS is still running underneath it, plus a written explanation of why a researched Type 1 hypervisor has no host OS and what that buys it in performance.

lessons.title: Virtual Machines: CPU, Memory & Storage Virtualization

slots.practicalActivity: In VirtualBox, open the settings for a VM and note its assigned vCPU count and RAM allocation, then check your own host machine's physical core count and total RAM, writing one sentence on whether the VM's allocation is a modest or an overcommitted share of the host's real resources. Create a new virtual disk for a VM and choose dynamically-allocated (thin-provisioned) sizing, then check the actual file size on the host disk right after creation versus the maximum size you set, confirming it hasn't pre-reserved the full amount.
slots.deliverable: A VM's real vCPU/RAM settings compared against your host machine's actual physical core count and RAM, plus a thin-provisioned virtual disk whose real file size on the host disk is shown to be smaller than its configured maximum right after creation.

lessons.title: Containers vs. Virtual Machines

slots.practicalActivity: Install Docker (Docker Desktop or the Linux engine in your lab VM) and run docker run --rm hello-world, timing roughly how long the container takes to start versus how long your VirtualBox VM took to boot in an earlier session. Then run docker run -d nginx and a second container from the same image, and use docker exec on each to confirm — via hostname or a process list — that they're isolated from each other even though both share your one host kernel.
slots.deliverable: A timed comparison between a Docker container's startup and a VM's boot time, plus 2 running containers from the same image confirmed as isolated from each other via docker exec.

lessons.title: Why Cloud Computing Is Built on Virtualization

slots.practicalActivity: Sign up for a free-tier AWS, Azure, or GCP account if you haven't already, launch (or configure) one small VM, and time how long it actually takes from clicking launch/create to the VM being reachable. Write 2-3 sentences explaining, using the lesson's own framing, why that was a software operation on an already-running hypervisor rather than new physical hardware being provisioned, and name the specific hypervisor platform (Nitro or Hyper-V) your chosen provider runs underneath it.
slots.deliverable: A real cloud VM launched from a free-tier account with the actual launch-to-ready time recorded, plus a written explanation naming the provider's underlying hypervisor platform and why launching took seconds rather than hours.

lessons.title: IaaS, PaaS & SaaS: The Cloud Service Models

slots.practicalActivity: In your cloud provider's console, find and name one real IaaS service (a raw VM product), one real PaaS service (a managed app-hosting product), and one SaaS product you already use daily (Microsoft 365, Google Workspace, Slack, etc.). Build your own 6-row by 3-column table, reusing the lesson's datacenter/virtualization/OS/runtime/application/data layers, and mark each cell Provider or You for all three of your chosen real services.
slots.deliverable: 3 real named services (one IaaS, one PaaS, one SaaS) from a cloud console or daily tools, plus a completed 6x3 layer-responsibility table marking Provider vs. You for each of the three.

lessons.title: The Shared Responsibility Model

slots.practicalActivity: Using your own cloud console (or the lesson's examples if you don't have resources running), write out, for a real IaaS VM, a managed database service, and a SaaS product you use, exactly which security tasks are the provider's job and which are yours — OS patching, data, IAM, and network config. Then write 2-3 sentences explaining, with your own hypothetical example, why a leaked access key or an open storage bucket is squarely the customer's responsibility and not the provider's.
slots.deliverable: A written 3-service breakdown (IaaS VM, managed database, SaaS product) of security tasks split between provider and customer, plus a written explanation of why a leaked key or open bucket is the customer's fault, not the provider's.

lessons.title: Public, Private & Hybrid Cloud

slots.practicalActivity: Research one real company or published case study that uses a hybrid cloud setup — a bank, hospital, or government agency connecting on-prem infrastructure to AWS/Azure via VPN or ExpressRoute/Direct Connect is a common example — and summarize their setup in 2-3 sentences, naming which of the lesson's 4 real business reasons (compliance, latency, legacy systems, gradual migration) actually drove their decision. Then write a one-paragraph recommendation for a fictional new startup with no existing datacenter and no unusual regulatory burden, explaining why public cloud alone is the right starting point for them.
slots.deliverable: A written 2-3 sentence summary of one real hybrid-cloud case study naming the specific business reason behind it, plus a one-paragraph recommendation for a startup explaining why public cloud alone fits their situation.

lessons.title: Regions, Availability Zones & Why They Matter

slots.practicalActivity: In a real AWS, Azure, or GCP console, browse the list of available regions and, for one region close to you, the list of Availability Zones inside it, writing down their real names (e.g. us-east-1a/1b/1c or Azure's zone 1/2/3). Design, on paper, a resiliency plan for a fictional 2-server web app: which region you'd pick and why, how many AZs you'd spread the 2 servers across, and whether a region pair is warranted yet, citing the specific risk each choice protects against.
slots.deliverable: Real region and Availability Zone names found in a cloud console, plus a written resiliency plan for a 2-server app naming the chosen region, the AZ spread, and whether a region pair is justified, with the risk each choice addresses.

lessons.title: Virtual Networks: VPCs and VNets

slots.practicalActivity: In a real AWS or Azure free-tier account, create one VPC or VNet with a CIDR block of your choosing (e.g. 10.0.0.0/16), and confirm in the console that nothing inside it can reach the internet yet by default. Write 2-3 sentences explaining why two unrelated companies could both choose the exact same 10.0.0.0/16 range without any conflict, and name one of the specific mechanisms (internet gateway, NAT gateway, VPN connection, or peering) you'd need to configure to deliberately open an outbound path.
slots.deliverable: A real VPC or VNet created in a free-tier cloud account with its CIDR block set, plus a written explanation of why two companies can share the same address range with no conflict and which mechanism would be needed to open outbound internet access.

lessons.title: Subnets, Routing Tables & Security Groups in the Cloud

slots.practicalActivity: Inside the VPC or VNet you created last session, carve out at least 2 subnets (e.g. a 10.0.1.0/24 public subnet and a 10.0.2.0/24 private subnet), and inspect each one's route table in the console, confirming which one has a route to an internet gateway and which doesn't — that's what actually makes one public and the other private, not a label. Then write one security group rule set, in the lesson's inbound/outbound format, for a web server allowing HTTPS from anywhere and SSH only from your own VPC's CIDR range, and explain in one sentence why a security group doesn't need a separate outbound rule for the HTTPS reply traffic.
slots.deliverable: 2 real subnets carved out of a VPC/VNet with their route tables inspected and labeled public/private based on the internet gateway route, plus a written security group rule set for a web server with an explanation of why stateful matching skips a separate outbound reply rule.

lessons.title: Load Balancing Fundamentals

slots.practicalActivity: If you have 2 small web servers available — 2 local python -m http.server instances, or 2 real cloud VMs — set up a real load balancer in front of them (an Nginx reverse proxy locally, or a real cloud load balancer if you have cloud resources) and send several repeated requests to confirm traffic alternates between both backends. Then write a 3-row Layer 7 routing table, like the lesson's /api/*, /images/*, / example, for a fictional app of your choosing, and explain in one sentence why that specific routing could only be done by a Layer 7 load balancer, not a Layer 4 one.
slots.deliverable: A real load balancer (Nginx or cloud-based) distributing requests across at least 2 backend servers, confirmed by repeated test requests, plus a written 3-row Layer 7 routing table with an explanation of why it requires Layer 7, not Layer 4.

lessons.title: Cloud Storage Types: Object, Block & File

slots.practicalActivity: If you have a free-tier cloud account, create one real object storage bucket (S3 or Blob Storage) and upload a test file to it via the console or CLI, noting that you addressed it by key/URL rather than a drive letter. Then write the lesson's 3-way comparison table (object/block/file) filled in with your own one-sentence justification for each, and apply it to 3 real scenarios of your choosing: a database's data files, a set of nightly backups, and a shared folder 3 web servers all need to write to at once.
slots.deliverable: A real object storage bucket with one uploaded test file (or, without a cloud account, the completed object/block/file comparison table alone), plus 3 real scenarios each correctly matched to object, block, or file storage with a one-sentence justification.

lessons.title: Lab: Provisioning and Networking a Linux VM End to End

slots.practicalActivity: Reproduce the Briarcliff lab for real: in a free-tier AWS or Azure account, generate your own SSH key pair with ssh-keygen -t ed25519, create a VNet/VPC with at least one subnet if you don't already have one from Chapter 7, launch a real Ubuntu Server VM into that subnet with your public key attached and no password set, and configure its security group/NSG with exactly one inbound rule for TCP port 22 scoped to your own current public IP, not 0.0.0.0/0. Connect with ssh -i, then run the lesson's first-login checklist: systemctl status sshd, sudo apt update && sudo apt upgrade, and a check of /var/log/auth.log confirming only your own login appears.
slots.deliverable: A real Ubuntu VM provisioned in a cloud VPC/VNet with SSH key-only access scoped to your own IP, connected to successfully, plus output from the full first-login checklist (sshd status, apt update/upgrade, and an auth.log check) confirming it's genuinely ready.

lessons.title: Foundations Capstone: Diagnosing a Connectivity Problem

slots.practicalActivity: Using the VM from last session (or a second one in the same subnet), deliberately misconfigure its security group/NSG's SSH rule to a source range that excludes your real current IP, then run the lesson's exact 5-step diagnostic sequence yourself: confirm the VM is running, list and inspect the security group rules, check the route table/effective routes, use console/serial access to check systemctl status sshd and /var/log/auth.log directly on the VM, and finally fix the one stale rule and confirm ssh connects immediately afterward.
slots.deliverable: A real, deliberately broken SSH security-group rule diagnosed through the full 5-step sequence (VM status, security group rules, route table, in-VM service/log check, and the fix), ending in a successful SSH connection after the one-line rule correction.

monthlyMilestoneContribution: A student finishing this course can read and subnet an IP address, explain exactly how a request travels from a laptop through DNS, DHCP, NAT, and a firewall to a server and back, work entirely from a Linux command line — navigating the filesystem, managing users, groups, permissions, and packages, controlling processes and systemd services, reading logs, and writing a real Bash script — and understands the cloud's own building blocks (hypervisors, containers, IaaS/PaaS/SaaS, the shared responsibility model, regions and Availability Zones, VPCs/VNets, subnets, security groups, load balancers, and storage types) well enough to have personally provisioned a real cloud Linux VM with SSH key-based access and diagnosed a real stale-security-group connectivity failure end to end — the exact networking, Linux, and cloud foundation every later course in this path assumes.
